question: Amid staunch opposition from Chios’ grassroots organisations, the Nea Dimokratia Government – together with the EU – is pursuing an investment in antimony mining that is dangerous both for public health and the environment. It is telling that antimony mining had stopped for decades. A large number of studies have noted the negative effect of antimony on the water table.

The Greek Government and the EU are prioritising support for corporate groups serving the war and renewable energy industries etc., providing subsidies through the Act on so-called ‘critical raw materials’. As a result, the environment and the health of local residents are being crushed in a stampede by European monopolistic groups, China and the US to make a profit.

Local residents have set up a coordinating committee and are continuing to mobilise and protest, supported by more than 100 local entities, as well as others such as the Greek Miners’ Federation. In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Where does it stand on the calls from residents and entities for a definitive end to all planning and actions linked to the antimony mining project in Chios, which poses a risk to the health of local residents and the environment?

Where does it stand on the fact that the EU’s Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), aimed at boosting the EU’s competitiveness and profitability vis-à-vis its rivals, involves mining activities that are harmful to people’s health and destructive towards the environment?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (8.9.2026) As regards the antimony mining plans referred to by the Honourable Member, the Commission has been made aware of them by written questions E-002085/20241, The Commission would like to remind that mining projects fall under the scope of Directive 2011/92/EU5.

Depending on their size, they are either subject to an assessment of the environmental effects or a determination if such an assessment is necessary, based on a caseby-case analysis or by setting specific criteria (such as the location, size or type of project) before their authorization.

Where an assessment is required, Members States shall therefore take into account the impacts of the projects on cultural heritage or environmental aspects and the opinion of the concerned public to ensure sustainable development.

Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, it is primarily the responsibility of the Greek authorities to ensure that projects are developed in full compliance with EU environmental legislation.

The Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA)6 was designed to strengthen and diversify the EU’s supply of strategic raw materials while fully maintaining the EU’s high standards for public health, environmental protection and public participation. The CRMA does not lower existing environmental safeguards.

Any mining project in the EU must continue to comply with the full body of applicable EU legislation, including requirements relating to environmental impact assessment, water protection, nature conservation, industrial emissions and public consultation.
